citeAs: Li, Y., Du, Y., Zhou, K., Wang, J., Zhao, W. X., & Wen, J.-R. (2023). Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv.
creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen (Renmin University of China; Meituan Group)
description: POPE is a polling-based object probing evaluation dataset/benchmark for measuring object hallucination in large vision-language models. It constructs image-question-answer triples from image datasets by asking yes/no questions such as whether a given object is present in an image, under random, popular, and adversarial negative sampling settings.
name: POPE
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper evaluates POPE with Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 score, compares prompt stability against CHAIR using multiple prompt templates, studies consistency between yes/no responses and generated captions, and compares annotation-based versus SEEM-based POPE results.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: POPE forms yes/no polling questions from objects in each image using the template "Is there a/an <object> in the image?" Ground-truth objects create positive questions, and nonexistent objects create negative questions, with a 1:1 balance between ground-truth and nonexistent objects. The paper defines three negative sampling strategies: random sampling, popular sampling using top frequent objects absent from the image, and adversarial sampling using top co-occurring objects absent from the image.
rai:dataCollection: Given an image caption dataset, POPE constructs triples consisting of an image, multiple object-probing questions, and yes/no answers. Objects to probe are obtained either from human annotations or automatic segmentation tools such as SEEM, and nonexistent objects are negatively sampled under random, popular, or adversarial settings.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data are images and object information from existing image datasets such as MSCOCO, and optionally segmentation outputs from SEEM used to identify objects in images.
rai:dataLimitations: The paper notes that POPE only evaluates object hallucination rather than overall LVLM capability; experiments use only part of each validation set due to computation limits; yes/no matching can be inaccurate when models do not explicitly answer with those words; automatic segmentation labels may diverge from human annotations; and only a small number of LVLMs were compared.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The benchmark applies negative sampling to create nonexistent-object questions under three settings: random sampling, popular sampling from top frequent objects absent from the image, and adversarial sampling from top co-occurring objects absent from the image. It also balances positive and negative questions at a 1:1 ratio.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Objects in images are first obtained from human annotations or automatic segmentation. POPE then samples nonexistent objects under random, popular, or adversarial settings and converts both present and absent objects into templated yes/no questions for each image.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper argues that object hallucination can hinder safe real-world use of large vision-language models and may cause unexpected consequences, such as wrong decisions in autonomous driving due to incorrect understanding of the external environment. The work aims to support development of more reliable and human-aligned LVLMs.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for evaluating object hallucination in large vision-language models, comparing hallucination behavior across models, and extending hallucination evaluation to datasets with or without human object annotations.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: SEEM for automatic segmentation-based object annotation; ChatGPT for parsing open-ended VQA responses during evaluation.
